flawed_step: Lines 0054-0063 (the case |R_{m-1}| < n/2): extending R_{m-1} to a half-size set S with R_{m-1} ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1} and then asserting on lines 0061-0063 that 'S is a subset of W_{m-1} with |S| = n/2 and crucially no neighbor in W_m (since S ⊇ R_{m-1}, and by construction R_{m-1} has no edges to W_m)'. Having no neighbor in W_m is not inherited upward from a subset to a superset; only R_{m-1} is known to have no neighbor in W_m, while the padding vertices of S \ R_{m-1} (vertices of W_{m-1} that are simply not reachable from W_1) may be adjacent to W_m. The auxiliary remark on line 0060, 'no vertex in S lies in W_m (indeed S ⊆ W_{m-1})', is also false, since W_{m-1} and W_m are both subsets of the same V of size ≥ (1-α)n and necessarily overlap heavily. Consequently N(S) ⊆ V \ W_m (line 0065) and |N(S)| ≤ αn (line 0067) are unjustified, and no contradiction is obtained in this case. (The correct argument instead maintains the invariant |R_i| ≥ n/2 for all i: if |R_{i-1}| ≥ n/2 then |N(R_{i-1})| ≥ n/2 + αn, so |R_i| = |N(R_{i-1}) ∩ W_i| ≥ (n/2 + αn) + (1-α)n - n = n/2; the small-R case the proof tries to handle never arises. The theorem is true; the proof of it is not.)
counterexample:
Witness that the inference at lines 0061-0063 is invalid (a concrete graph satisfying every hypothesis of the problem, together with concrete R ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1} where R has no neighbor in W_m but S does):

n = 8, α = 1/8, so n/2 = 4, the expansion requirement is |N(S)| ≥ n/2 + αn = 4 + 1 = 5 for every S with |S| = 4, and the size requirement on the W_i is |W_i| ≥ (1-α)n = 7.

V = {1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8}. E = all 21 edges of the complete graph on {2,3,4,5,6,7,8}, plus the single edge {1,2}. So deg(1) = 1 with N({1}) = {2}.

Expansion check (using N(S) = {w : ∃ v ∈ S, (v,w) ∈ E} as in the problem, so N(S) may meet S):
 - If S ⊆ {2,...,8} with |S| = 4: every vertex of {2,...,8} is adjacent to some element of S (the clique is complete and |S| = 4 ≥ 2), so N(S) ⊇ {2,...,8} and |N(S)| ≥ 7 ≥ 5.
 - If 1 ∈ S, say S = {1} ∪ T with T ⊆ {2,...,8}, |T| = 3: N(S) = {2} ∪ N(T) ⊇ {2,...,8}, so |N(S)| ≥ 7 ≥ 5.
So the expansion hypothesis holds (with room to spare).

Now take the two consecutive layers
  W_{m-1} = {1,3,4,5,6,7,8}  (|W_{m-1}| = 7 ≥ 7),
  W_m     = {1,3,4,5,6,7,8}  (|W_m| = 7 ≥ 7),
both legal choices, and take R := {1} ⊆ W_{m-1}, which is nonempty with |R| = 1 < n/2 = 4 — exactly the situation of lines 0054-0059.

R has no neighbor in W_m: N(R) = N({1}) = {2}, and 2 ∉ W_m. So R satisfies the hypothesis the proof carries into this case.

The proof now pads R up to size n/2 = 4 inside W_{m-1}. Every such padding fails its conclusion; take for instance the choice
  S = {1,3,4,5},  so R ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1} and |S| = 4 = n/2,
exactly as the proof prescribes. Then
  N(S) = N({1}) ∪ N({3,4,5}) = {2} ∪ {2,3,4,5,6,7,8} = {2,3,4,5,6,7,8},
and therefore
  N(S) ∩ W_m = {3,4,5,6,7,8} ≠ ∅.
So S DOES have neighbors in W_m, refuting the claim on lines 0062-0063; N(S) ⊆ V \ W_m (line 0065) is false, since 3 ∈ N(S) ∩ W_m; and the numeric conclusion |N(S)| ≤ αn (line 0067) is false by a wide margin: |N(S)| = 7 while αn = 1. Indeed |N(S)| = 7 ≥ 5 obeys the expansion property, so no contradiction arises. Line 0060's parenthetical is refuted by the same data: 3, 4, 5 ∈ S and 3, 4, 5 ∈ W_m.

Moreover no other padding rescues the step: any S with {1} ⊆ S ⊆ W_{m-1} and |S| = 4 must contain three vertices of {3,...,8} ⊆ W_m, each of which is adjacent to all of {2,...,8} and hence to vertices of W_m. So in this instance every S the proof is allowed to construct has |N(S)| = 7 > αn = 1, and the case |R_{m-1}| < n/2 yields no contradiction at all.
reasoning_summary: Verified in order. Lines 0002-0018 (base case k = 2) are sound: if no W_1-W_2 edge existed, any S ⊆ W_1 with |S| = n/2 (which exists since α ≤ 1/2 is forced by n/2 + αn ≤ |N(S)| ≤ n, so |W_1| ≥ (1-α)n ≥ n/2) would have N(S) ⊆ V \ W_2 of size ≤ αn, contradicting |N(S)| ≥ n/2 + αn. Lines 0019-0037 correctly set up the layered digraph and the reachability sets R_1 = W_1, R_i = N(R_{i-1}) ∩ W_i. Lines 0038-0047 are correct: absence of a layered path gives R_k = ∅, a minimal m with R_m = ∅ exists with 2 ≤ m ≤ k, and by minimality every vertex of R_{m-1} has no neighbor in W_m. Lines 0048-0053 (case |R_{m-1}| ≥ n/2) are correct, since any S ⊆ R_{m-1} of size n/2 satisfies N(S) ⊆ N(R_{m-1}), which misses W_m. The proof fails at lines 0054-0063 (case |R_{m-1}| < n/2): after padding R_{m-1} with arbitrary vertices of W_{m-1} to reach size n/2, it asserts the enlarged set S still has no neighbor in W_m 'since S ⊇ R_{m-1}'. That is a monotonicity error in the wrong direction — the added vertices are merely unreachable from W_1, not non-adjacent to W_m — and the supporting remark that S ⊆ W_{m-1} keeps S disjoint from W_m is also false, as W_{m-1} and W_m are overlapping large subsets of the same V. Hence lines 0065 and 0067 are unjustified and the intended contradiction is not obtained in this case, which is precisely the case the whole inductive step needed. The explicit witness (n = 8, α = 1/8, K_7 on {2,...,8} plus the pendant edge {1,2}, W_{m-1} = W_m = {1,3,...,8}, R = {1}, S = {1,3,4,5}) satisfies all problem hypotheses and shows the step's conclusion failing: |N(S)| = 7 while the step claims |N(S)| ≤ αn = 1. The stated theorem is nevertheless true — the correct proof carries the invariant |R_i| ≥ n/2 forward, so the gap is a genuine defect in this argument rather than a false statement.
